docs.title: Spring AI Decision Extensions
docs.text: Higher-level building blocks on top of the Spring AI DecisionModel API: a model-as-a-judge made of atomic questions, self-refine and guardrail advisors for ChatClient, and a chat model adapter for typed classifications.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Most AI code coerces a text-generation model into emitting structured decisions, then parses the results back into something the program can depend on. That round trip is where the failures live: the model answers in a shape the parser did not expect, a rating drifts between runs, and a single overall score hides the one defect that mattered.

A decision model is not a chat model. It takes an input and a map of typed questions, and returns structured answers: no text generation, no JSON to coerce, no parsing. Every question in a call is answered against the same input, so the pattern is atomic questions, composed in code rather than one broad rubric prompt.

DecisionResponse response = decisionModel.call(DecisionPrompt.builder()
        .text("Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.")
        .question("is_urgent",   YesNoQuestion.of("Does this convey urgency?"))
        .question("department",  ChoiceQuestion.builder()
                .text("Which team should handle this?")
                .option("billing",   "Payments, invoicing, refunds")
                .option("technical", "Bugs, outages, integrations")
                .option("sales",     "Pricing, upgrades, new accounts")
                .build())
        .question("frustration", ScoreQuestion.of("How frustrated is the customer?",
                "Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"))
        .build());

double urgency     = response.getYesNo("is_urgent").getProbability();   // 0.95
String department  = response.getChoice("department").getValue();       // "billing"
Double confidence  = response.getChoice("department").getConfidence();  // 0.82
double frustration = response.getScore("frustration").getValue();       // 1.1

That API ships with Spring AI. This project adds what you build on top of it:

  • DecisionJudge: a model-as-a-judge built from atomic criteria instead of one rubric prompt, each with its own threshold, all in one model call
  • DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor: a ChatClient advisor that judges every response and retries the ones that fall short
  • DecisionGuardrailAdvisor: advisors that screen the user message and the reply against a battery of hazards
  • DecisionChatModel: a decision model behind the ChatModel interface, so ChatClient.entity(...) returns a typed classification
  • Patterns for acting on answers: a confidence gate, a consistency sampler and a composite score

They depend only on the DecisionModel API, not on a provider, so they work with any implementation: Ollama, OpenAI or System One.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
1. Import the BOM and add the artifacts you use:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-bom</artifactId>
            <version>0.5.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-self-refine</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-guardrail</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

The BOM keeps the artifacts on one version, so they cannot drift apart from each other.

2. Add a decision model. Any Spring AI provider works. The quickest to try is Ollama, which runs on your machine and needs no API key:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-model-ollama</artifactId>
</dependency>

ollama pull d1-omni:600m

The starter contributes a DecisionModel bean. See Providers for OpenAI and System One.

3. Judge, retry and screen a chat:

@Bean
ChatClient chatClient(ChatModel chatModel, DecisionModel decisionModel) {

    DecisionJudge judge = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
        .score("helpfulness", ScoreQuestion.builder()
                .text("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
                .level("Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic")
                .level("Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point")
                .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps remain")
                .level("Excellent: fully and correctly addressed")
                .build(), 2.0)
        .yesNo("is_plausible", YesNoQuestion.builder()
                .text("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
                .whenNo("Contains an impossible or absurd value")
                .build(), 0.7)
        .build();

    return ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
        .defaultAdvisors(
                DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.input(decisionModel),
                DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder().judge(judge).maxRepeatAttempts(3).build(),
                DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.output(decisionModel))
        .build();
}

Every answer the model gives is screened, then judged against both criteria, and retried with the defect as feedback when it falls short.

docs.title: Coming from spring-ai-typesafe
docs.text:
These components started in spring-ai-typesafe, where they were built on the TypeSafe client. Since Spring AI 2.1 the framework has its own DecisionModel API, with TypeSafe's System One protocol as one provider among several. This project is the same components re-implemented on that API.

What that buys: the judge, the advisors and the chat adapter now work with any DecisionModel, not only TypeSafe.

docs.text:
// spring-ai-typesafe
JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
    .noul("is_plausible", Noul.builder()
        .instructions("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
        .whenFalse("At least one value is impossible")
        .build(), 0.7d)
    .build();

// here
DecisionJudge judge = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .yesNo("is_plausible", YesNoQuestion.builder()
        .text("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
        .whenNo("At least one value is impossible")
        .build(), 0.7d)
    .build();

docs.title: What behaves differently
docs.text: Most of the port is a rename. These are the places where behaviour changed, and why.

docs.title: Because the API is provider-neutral
docs.text:
• Confidence can be missing. getConfidence() is null when a provider reports none. The confidence gate escalates such an answer, and the judge reads the probabilities rather than the confidence.
  • A provider can refuse one question. The judge reports a refused criterion as ERROR. The guardrail blocks the turn on a refused hazard. The chat adapter replies null for it.
  • There is no common outage exception. The self-refine advisor no longer recognises TypeSafeException. It takes a transientErrorPredicate, whose default covers I/O failures, timeouts and Spring AI's TransientAiException.
  • No batch API. DecisionConsistency fans its samples out itself; Sampling replaces JevBatchOptions.
  • No legend on a score. DecisionCompositeScore reads a rubric's height from the answer's probabilities, or from the question with of(response, questions).
  • The chat adapter's provider name is decision unless you set provider(...); it was always typesafe.

docs.title: Because the behaviour was wrong or risky
docs.text:
• A failing score's feedback no longer contradicts itself. With a fractional minimum, the feedback could read "rated 1.30, needs to reach 1.20". It now quotes the level the minimum counts from. The pass rule itself is unchanged: at least half of the probability on the levels at or above the minimum. See how a verdict is decided.
  • A hazard keeps its own action. A self-harm signal that is borderline but serious, or refused on review, now gets the support message instead of the plain refusal.
  • Input and output screening are separate advisors. DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.input(...) runs before chat memory, so a blocked message is never remembered and the battery sees what the person wrote. The single-advisor builder still works as before.
  • A retry is told more. The self-refine advisor's retry message now carries the rejected answer and the defects of earlier attempts, not only the latest feedback.
  • A retry that asks for a tool ends refining at the default order, where it used to restart the advisor and escape maxRepeatAttempts.
  • The tool-call-limit notice is not judged or retried, and neither is a reply a guardrail refused (any GuardrailRefusal, such as from SafeGuardAdvisor) or one the provider filtered.
  • Format instructions are removed only on an exact match in DecisionChatModel, and never on the native structured-output path, so user text cannot be cut by quoting them.
  • DecisionConsistency rejects a uid field of your own instead of overwriting it.

docs.title: DecisionChatModel
docs.text:
A decision model behind Spring AI's ChatModel interface, so a ChatClient can return typed classifications: which team, how urgent, how severe.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-chat</artifactId>
</dependency>

Experimental

DecisionChatModel is a prototype. Its name and behaviour may change. It lives in its own artifact so that it can change without touching the judge or the advisors.

docs.title: A classifier, not a generator
docs.text:
A ChatModel normally takes messages and generates a message. A decision model takes an input and answers typed questions with numbers. DecisionChatModel keeps the decision model what it is:

  • The questions are fixed when the model is built. The prompt only supplies the input they are answered against. Nothing is inferred from prose.
  • The reply is the answers as a JSON object, one field per question. ChatClient.entity(...) maps that straight onto a record.
  • What a decision model cannot do is refused, not faked. It doesn't stream, never calls tools and, by default, classifies text only. Probabilities and confidence stay in metadata, not in the reply text.

Use it where a fast label, flag or level is what the caller needs: routing, triage, moderation, intent detection, or any step in a workflow that only accepts a ChatModel.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
record Triage(String team, double urgent, double severity) {}

DecisionChatModel triage = DecisionChatModel.builder(decisionModel)
    .question("team", ChoiceQuestion.builder()
        .text("Which team should handle the user's ticket?")
        .option("infra", "Deploys, outages, servers and errors in production")
        .option("billing", "Invoices, payments, refunds and pricing")
        .option("support", "How-to questions and account help")
        .build())
    .question("urgent", YesNoQuestion.builder()
        .text("Does the user's ticket need attention right now?")
        .whenYes("Customers are affected now")
        .whenNo("It can wait for normal working hours")
        .build())
    .question("severity", ScoreQuestion.of("How severe is the impact described in the ticket?",
        "Cosmetic", "Degraded for some users", "Full outage"))
    .build();

Triage t = ChatClient.create(triage)
    .prompt()
    .user("Production is down after the 14:00 deploy; every customer gets HTTP 500.")
    .call()
    .entity(Triage.class, spec -> spec.useProviderStructuredOutput());
// e.g. Triage[team=infra, urgent=0.97, severity=1.8]

Name each question after the record component its answer should land in.

docs.title: Structured output
docs.text:
ChatClient.entity(...) asks for JSON in one of two ways, and the difference decides what the decision model sees and what is checked before the call:

sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant CC as ChatClient
    participant Adv as ChatModelCallAdvisor
    participant DCM as DecisionChatModel
    participant DM as DecisionModel

    App->>CC: entity(Triage.class, spec)
    alt native: spec.useProviderStructuredOutput()
        CC->>Adv: record's JSON schema
        Adv->>DCM: call(prompt) with the schema in the options
        DCM->>DCM: check the schema against the questions<br/>(a mismatch fails here, before any model call)
    else prompt-based: plain entity(Triage.class)
        CC->>Adv: format instructions
        Adv->>DCM: call(prompt) with the instructions appended to the last user message
        DCM->>DCM: remove the appended instructions from the input
    end
    DCM->>DM: input {system, messages} and the questions
    DM-->>DCM: DecisionResponse
    DCM-->>Adv: answers as a JSON object<br/>(only the record's fields when a schema was given)
    Adv-->>CC: ChatResponse
    CC-->>App: Triage record

spec.useProviderStructuredOutput() selects Spring AI's native structured output: the record's JSON schema reaches DecisionChatModel in the options. Prefer it:

  • The input is exactly what the caller wrote. Nothing is appended to the user message, so nothing is removed from it either.
  • The record is checked against the questions before any call. A field with no question of the same name fails with an IllegalArgumentException that names the field and lists the questions. So does a field whose type cannot hold the answer. A choice's option needs a String, or an enum that contains every option. A yes/no probability or a score's value needs a floating-point type (double, Double, float); int and boolean are rejected. Shared enums (a $ref in the schema) and nullable fields are followed, and so is a schema whose top level is itself a $ref. A field whose schema declares no type is accepted without a check.
  • The reply holds exactly the record's fields. Questions the record does not ask for are still answered, and are available in the metadata, but are left out of the reply. That keeps spec.validateSchema() working, since the schema forbids additional properties.
  • The target must be a single object. A record or class is fine; a List<...> target, or a schema that offers several alternative shapes at its top level, is rejected before any call.

With plain .entity(Triage.class), Spring AI uses prompt-based structured output instead. It appends format instructions to the last user message, and the default input removes them again. There is no schema check, and the reply contains every answer.

docs.title: What is removed, and what never is
docs.text:
The instructions are removed only when the message ends with exactly the block Spring AI's BeanOutputConverter or MapOutputConverter produces. The wording is read from those converters at runtime rather than copied, so it follows the Spring AI version in use.

This is deliberately strict, because the text of a user message is what gets classified. A message that merely quotes one of the format sentences, or carries text after them, is the user's content and is sent in full. Otherwise a user could hide text from a moderation classifier by writing those sentences in front of it.

ListOutputConverter is rejected, since it asks for comma-separated values, which a JSON object cannot satisfy. It is recognised the same strict way, and never on the native path.

One limit of the strict match

A user who appends a complete, well-formed copy of the format block to their own message still has that block removed, including any text placed inside its JSON schema. On the native path nothing is ever removed, which is one more reason to prefer it.

docs.title: What comes back
docs.text:
The reply is a JSON object, one field per question, in declaration order. With native structured output it holds only the record's fields.

Question Field value Example YesNoQuestion the probability of yes, 0..1 "urgent": 0.97 ChoiceQuestion the selected option "team": "infra" ScoreQuestion its value on the rubric, 0.. highest level "severity": 1.8 a question the model refused null "team": null 
String json = ChatClient.create(triage).prompt().user(ticket).call().content();
// {"team":"infra","urgent":0.97,"severity":1.8}

The full DecisionResponse, with every answer, probability and confidence, is in the generation metadata. The response metadata carries the model, the token usage and, when the provider reports one, the response id:

ChatResponse response = ChatClient.create(triage).prompt().user(ticket).call().chatResponse();

DecisionResponse decision = response.getResult().getMetadata().get(DecisionChatModel.RESPONSE_METADATA_KEY);
Double infra = decision.getChoice("team").getProbability("infra");   // null when not reported

response.getMetadata().getModel();
response.getMetadata().getUsage().getPromptTokens();

docs.title: What the decision model sees
docs.text:
By default, the prompt becomes a fields input:

{
  "system": "Tickets come from enterprise customers.",
  "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Production is down after ..." } ]
}
  • system (DecisionChatModel.SYSTEM_FIELD) holds every system message, joined with a blank line. It is left out when there are none.
  • messages (DecisionChatModel.MESSAGES_FIELD) holds the user and assistant turns, in order.
  • Format instructions: on the prompt-based path, the instructions appended to the last user message are removed, as described above. Earlier messages are left untouched.
  • Media: a message carrying media is rejected with IllegalArgumentException. The default input carries text only.

Write the questions in terms of that input, for example "the user's ticket". To judge a different shape, or to send media to a provider that reads it, supply your own converter:

DecisionChatModel.builder(decisionModel)
    .questions(questions)
    .inputConverter(prompt -> DecisionInput.fields(Map.of("ticket",
        DecisionChatModel.withoutFormatInstructions(prompt.getUserMessage().getText()))))
    .build();

A custom converter receives the prompt as sent. On the prompt-based path that includes the appended format instructions, so remove them with DecisionChatModel.withoutFormatInstructions, as above, or use native structured output. A converter can return any DecisionInput, including DecisionInput.conversation(...).

docs.title: Builder Configuration
docs.text:
Builder method Default Description question(String, DecisionQuestion) — (at least one) A question every call answers. The name is the reply's field. questions(Map<String, ? extends DecisionQuestion>) — Several questions at once, in map order. options(DecisionOptions) the model's defaults Options sent with every call. Their model name is also what getOptions() and the observations report. inputConverter(Function<Prompt, DecisionInput>) DecisionChatModel::defaultInput How a prompt becomes the input. answerRenderer(Function<DecisionResponse, String>) DecisionChatModel::answersAsJson How the answers become the reply's text. A custom renderer owns the reply's shape, so the native schema check is skipped. provider(String) "decision" The provider name reported on observations. observationRegistry(ObservationRegistry) ObservationRegistry.NOOP Observe each call; see observability. observationConvention(ChatModelObservationConvention) DefaultChatModelObservationConvention Replace the observation's name and key values.

A model named in the prompt's ChatOptions is used for that call; otherwise the one in the builder's options(...), and failing that the decision model's own default.

docs.title: What it refuses
docs.text:
Chat-model feature DecisionChatModel stream(...) errors with UnsupportedOperationException. A decision model answers every question at once. Tools given to ChatClient dropped. getOptions() are not tool-calling options, so ChatClient never starts its tool loop. A Prompt carrying tool callbacks directly rejected with IllegalArgumentException. Media in a message rejected with IllegalArgumentException by the default input. List output (ListOutputConverter) rejected with IllegalArgumentException. Temperature, top-p, max tokens ignored; a decision model has no such settings.

Advisors still run. Memory or retrieval advisors only add text to the input, though; they don't make the model generate anything.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Each call is observed like any other Spring AI chat model: a gen_ai.client.operation observation, contextually named chat <model>.

Key Value gen_ai.operation.name chat gen_ai.system decision (DecisionChatModel.DEFAULT_PROVIDER), or the builder's provider(...) gen_ai.request.model the model sent: the prompt's, or the builder's options' gen_ai.response.model the model that answered, when the provider reports it gen_ai.response.id the response id, when the provider reports it gen_ai.response.finish_reasons always ["STOP"] gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / output_tokens / total_tokens the token counts the decision model reports

The DecisionModel API does not say which provider is behind a model, so name it yourself when it matters in your dashboards:

DecisionChatModel.builder(decisionModel)
    .questions(questions)
    .provider("ollama")
    .observationRegistry(observationRegistry)
    .build();

With Spring AI's ChatModelMeterObservationHandler registered, token usage is also recorded as gen_ai.client.token.usage. The decision model's own decision observation nests inside this one.

docs.title: With Spring Boot
docs.text:
Expose a ChatClient built on the model, not the model itself. Pass the ObservationRegistry to both, so the ChatClient and advisor observations are recorded alongside the model's:

@Bean
ChatClient triageClient(DecisionModel decisionModel, ObservationRegistry observationRegistry) {
    DecisionChatModel triage = DecisionChatModel.builder(decisionModel)
        .questions(TRIAGE_QUESTIONS)
        .observationRegistry(observationRegistry)
        .build();
    return ChatClient.create(triage, observationRegistry);
}

Do not declare a DecisionChatModel bean

A DecisionChatModel is a ChatModel. Declared as a bean next to the application's real model, it makes two ChatModel beans. Then any injection of Spring AI's auto-configured ChatClient.Builder, or of a bare ChatModel, fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Marking the real model @Primary removes the error, but leaves a classifier registered as a ChatModel for anything that collects them all; marking the DecisionChatModel @Primary makes every other ChatClient use it silently. Build the model inside the method that creates its ChatClient, as above, and inject that client by name.

The DecisionModel bean comes from the provider's starter.

docs.title: When to use something else
docs.text:
• A verdict on a model's answer, with thresholds and feedback: DecisionJudge.
  • Judging and retrying inside a chat call: DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.
  • No ChatClient needed: call the DecisionModel directly. It is the same request, without the adapter.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: Confidence is a second axis. The answer tells you what; confidence tells you whether to act on it unattended.

docs.title: What it actually measures
docs.text:
ChoiceAnswer and ScoreAnswer carry getConfidence(): the provider's own estimate, between 0 and 1, of how sure it is about the whole answer. It reflects how well the options or levels separated for this input.

A low value is not the same as the answer being wrong. It means the question did not decide cleanly, which is a different problem and wants a different response: not "reject this answer", but "do not let software act on this one alone".

Yes/no answers carry no confidence, by design

A yes/no answer's probability already is its certainty. A 0.5 is the undecided case, so there is nothing a separate statistic would add. Only choices and scores report confidence.

Confidence can be missing

getConfidence() is null when the provider doesn't report it, and with Ollama and System One a value of 0 can also mean "none reported". The components here treat a missing confidence as the cautious case: the gate escalates, and the judge reads the probabilities rather than the confidence.

docs.title: Two things read it
docs.text:
The gate and the judge are the two components that act on certainty, and they ask different questions of it.

        +getConfidence() Double

    class ScoreAnswer {

docs.title: Confidence-gated routing
docs.text:
Tier your thresholds by what the action costs when it is wrong. A universal floor keeps anything genuinely undecided away from automation; above it, expensive actions demand more than cheap ones.

DecisionConfidenceGate holds that policy in one place:

DecisionConfidenceGate gate = DecisionConfidenceGate.builder()
    .floor(0.60d)                     // nothing acts unattended below this
    .require("transfer_funds", 0.85d) // this one costs more when wrong
    .build();

switch (gate.decide(response.getChoice("intent"))) {
    case EXECUTE  -> perform(intent);
    case CONFIRM  -> askTheUserToConfirm(intent);
    case ESCALATE -> handOverToAHuman();
}

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App
    participant Gate as DecisionConfidenceGate
    participant Human

    App->>Gate: decide(response.getChoice("intent"))

    alt confidence missing, or below the floor
        Gate-->>App: ESCALATE
        App->>Human: hand over
    else below the action's own requirement
        Gate-->>App: CONFIRM
        App->>Human: ask to confirm
    else at or above the requirement
        Gate-->>App: EXECUTE
        App->>App: perform(intent)
    end

The two thresholds are independent: the floor is about the answer being undecided at all, the per-action requirement is about what the action costs when it is wrong.

Confidence Low-stakes action High-stakes action missing, or below the floor escalate escalate floor … requirement execute ask the user to confirm at or above requirement execute execute

Thresholds are properties of the model that answers. Tuned on one model, they don't carry over to another provider; measure them again there.

docs.title: Confidence in the judge
docs.text:
DecisionJudge makes a pass/fail decision, so it asks a narrower question than getConfidence() does. Not how sure is the provider about the answer? but how much of the probability supports this verdict?: the probability on the verdict's side of the threshold.

The two differ when the probability is split between levels that all pass, or all fail. Probabilities of 0.52 on level 2 and 0.41 on level 3, against a minimum of 2, come with a confidence near 0.5, yet 93% of the probability supports the pass.

A criterion whose verdict is not supported by enough probability is undecided, not failed. It is reported as INCONCLUSIVE and does not block:

DecisionJudge judge = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .score("helpfulness", rubric, 2.0d)
    .minConfidence(0.6d)          // the default: a clear majority must support the verdict
    .failOnInconclusive(false)    // the default: undecided does not block
    .build();

When the provider reports no probabilities, the judge uses the answer's own confidence instead. When it reports neither, there is nothing to gate on and the answer is acted on as given.

DecisionConfidenceGate still reads getConfidence() itself, because routing an action is a different decision: there, how clearly one option won is exactly the question.

Turn failOnInconclusive(true) on where shipping an unverified answer is worse than failing. Leaving it off is right when an occasional unverifiable answer is acceptable and a false rejection is not.

docs.title: Stability is a different question
docs.text:
Confidence describes one answer. It says nothing about whether you would get the same answer again, and a value that lands near a threshold may be noise rather than judgement.

DecisionConsistency answers that by sampling:

DecisionConsistency.Report report = DecisionConsistency.sample(decisionModel, fields, questions, 15);

// The questions whose samples straddle the threshold you are about to rely on
List<String> shaky = report.unstableAt(0.70d);

A criterion whose samples fall on both sides of its threshold makes a decision that is not reproducible. Either move the threshold, sharpen the question, or route that case to a human.

docs.title: Decision Models
docs.text: Everything in this project is built on the Spring AI DecisionModel API. This page is a short tour of it; the Spring AI reference is the full description.

docs.title: What a decision model is
docs.text:
Many decisions in an application have a small, known set of possible results: yes or no, one of a few categories, or a level on a scale. You could ask a chat model, but it answers with free text, and you must turn that text into a reliable yes or no yourself.

A decision model is made for these decisions. You describe the possible results, and the model picks one and tells you how likely each result is. It is usually faster and cheaper than a chat model asked the same thing, and because it reports probabilities, your application decides how sure the model must be before it acts.

Still a model, not a rule engine

A decision model's answers are not deterministic, and they can be wrong. For each decision, think about what happens when the answer is wrong. When a mistake is expensive, let a person check the answer or use a safe default.

docs.title: Asking questions
docs.text:
A DecisionPrompt holds the input, the questions to ask about it and, optionally, the settings of the call.

DecisionResponse response = decisionModel.call(DecisionPrompt.builder()
    .text("My new headphones arrived yesterday, but the left side doesn't work. Can I get my money back?")
    .question("defect", YesNoQuestion.builder()
        .text("Does the customer report a defect?")
        .whenYes("Part of the item does not work as it should")
        .whenNo("The item works, and the message is about something else")
        .build())
    .question("topic", ChoiceQuestion.builder()
        .text("What is the message about?")
        .option("delivery", "Where an order is, or when it will arrive")
        .option("product", "A problem with an item the customer received")
        .option("account", "Login, address or payment details")
        .option("other", "None of the above")
        .build())
    .question("satisfaction", ScoreQuestion.of("How satisfied is the customer?", "unhappy", "neutral", "happy"))
    .build());

boolean defect = response.getYesNo("defect").isYes();
String topic = response.getChoice("topic").getValue();
int satisfaction = response.getScore("satisfaction").getNearestLevel();

When you have only a text and one or two questions, call(String, Map) is shorter:

DecisionResponse response = decisionModel.call("Where is my order? I ordered it two weeks ago.",
        Map.of("topic", ChoiceQuestion.of("What is the message about?",
                "delivery", "product", "account", "other")));

docs.title: The three questions
docs.text:
There are three kinds of questions, and every provider supports all three. Each answers differently, and each is thresholded differently, which is the reason to pick deliberately between them.

Question What it asks Answer YesNoQuestion Whether something is true. Optional whenYes and whenNo criteria say what counts as a yes and what counts as a no. YesNoAnswer, with the probability of yes ChoiceQuestion Which of the offered options fits the input. Each option has a name and, optionally, a description. ChoiceAnswer, with the selected option and, when the provider reports them, the probability of each option ScoreQuestion Which level of an ordered scale fits the input. Each level has a label and, optionally, a description. ScoreAnswer, with the expected level and, when the provider reports them, the probability of each level 
classDiagram
    direction TB

    class DecisionQuestion {
        <<sealed interface>>
        +getText() String
    }

    class YesNoQuestion {
        +getWhenYes() String
        +getWhenNo() String
        +of(String)$ YesNoQuestion
    }

    class ChoiceQuestion {
        +getOptions() Map
        +getOptionNames() List~String~
        +of(String, String...)$ ChoiceQuestion
    }

    class ScoreQuestion {
        +getLevels() List~ScoreLevel~
        +of(String, String...)$ ScoreQuestion
    }

    DecisionQuestion <|.. YesNoQuestion
    DecisionQuestion <|.. ChoiceQuestion
    DecisionQuestion <|.. ScoreQuestion

    note for ChoiceQuestion "named options; unordered"
    note for ScoreQuestion "ordered levels; the index is the level"

DecisionQuestion and DecisionAnswer are sealed interfaces. A switch over a question or an answer can cover every kind, and the compiler checks that none is missing.

docs.title: Yes/no
docs.text:
A yes/no question's answer is a probability rather than a boolean. There is no separate confidence, because a probability of 0.5 already tells you the model is undecided.

Adding whenYes and whenNo descriptions is what turns a vague question into a usable one. They also become the defect text a judge feeds back, so write them as statements about the input rather than instructions to a model:

YesNoQuestion plausible = YesNoQuestion.builder()
    .text("Are all the numeric values physically plausible for their units?")
    .whenYes("Every value is within a range that can actually occur")
    .whenNo("At least one value is impossible, such as a temperature below absolute zero")
    .build();

docs.title: Choice
docs.text:
A choice picks exactly one option from a fixed set.

A choice always names an option

A ChoiceAnswer names an option even when none of them fits. When "none of these" is a real outcome in your domain, ask it as a separate YesNoQuestion next to the choice, or add an explicit other option.

docs.title: Score
docs.text:
A score places the input on an ordered rubric you define. Its value is continuous: the expected level, weighted by the probabilities. A 1.1 on a three-level rubric sits just past the second level, leaning toward the third.

Because the value is continuous, a threshold of 2.0 is a real threshold and not a rounding artefact. Keep the levels genuinely ordered. If two levels are alternatives rather than degrees, you want a choice.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The input is what the questions are about. DecisionInput offers three kinds, and the DecisionPrompt builder has a method for each.

Input Use it for text(String) A plain text, such as a customer message. For a text with images, use content(MessagePart...). fields(Map) An input made of named fields. The model gets each value with its name, so it knows what each value means. Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, nulls, maps and lists. conversation(List<Message>) A conversation, made of the same Message types that a ChatModel takes. Use it to check an exchange. 
Map<String, Object> customer = new LinkedHashMap<>();
customer.put("message", "This is the third time my order arrives late.");
customer.put("orders", 12);
customer.put("late_deliveries", 3);

DecisionResponse repeated = decisionModel.call(DecisionInput.fields(customer),
        Map.of("repeated", YesNoQuestion.of("Does the customer say that the problem happened before?")));

Naming a field in a question's text (`message`) is how you point a question at one part of a fields input instead of the whole thing. The judge and the guardrail both work this way: their questions refer to assistant_answer, tool_calls or text by name.

Use a LinkedHashMap for fields

The model reads the fields in the order they are sent, and some models answer differently when that order changes. Map.of(...) has no order, so it can change between JVM runs.

Not every provider supports every kind of input or content part, such as images. See Providers.

docs.title: Reading answers
docs.text:
A DecisionResponse holds one answer for each question, and the metadata of the call. Get an answer by its name, with the method for its kind: getYesNo(name), getChoice(name) or getScore(name).

classDiagram
    direction TB

    class DecisionAnswer {
        <<sealed interface>>
    }

    class YesNoAnswer {
        +getProbability() double
        +isYes() boolean
        +isYes(double) boolean
    }

    class ChoiceAnswer {
        +getValue() String
        +getProbabilities() Map
        +getRankedOptions() List
        +getConfidence() Double
    }

    class ScoreAnswer {
        +getValue() double
        +getNearestLevel() int
        +getProbabilities() List
        +getConfidence() Double

    class RefusalAnswer {
        +getReason() String
    }

    DecisionAnswer <|.. YesNoAnswer
    DecisionAnswer <|.. ChoiceAnswer
    DecisionAnswer <|.. ScoreAnswer
    DecisionAnswer <|.. RefusalAnswer

    note for YesNoAnswer "no confidence:<br/>the probability is the certainty"

Yes/no. getProbability() is the probability of yes. isYes() answers yes at 0.5 or above; with isYes(double) you choose the threshold:

// open a repair ticket automatically only when the model is very sure
boolean defect = response.getYesNo("defect").isYes(0.9);

Choice. getValue() is the selected option. When the provider reports them, getProbability(option) and getRankedOptions() give the probability of each option. If the selected option is only a little more likely than the second one, the input is not clear, and a person may handle it better.

Score. There are three ways to read a score:

  • getNearestLevel(): the position of the most likely level, starting at 0. Use this one to act on.
  • getValue(): the expected level, the average level weighted by the probabilities. A decimal number between 0 and the number of levels minus one.
  • getRoundedLevel(): the expected level, rounded to the nearest level.

The expected level can be a level that the model thinks is unlikely:

// probabilities 0.5, 0, 0.5 over the levels unhappy, neutral, happy
ScoreAnswer satisfaction = response.getScore("satisfaction");
satisfaction.getNearestLevel();  // 0, unhappy: as likely as happy, and the first one wins
satisfaction.getValue();         // 1.0, the average level weighted by the probabilities
satisfaction.getRoundedLevel();  // 1, neutral, which has no probability at all

docs.title: Probabilities and confidence
docs.text:
The probabilities are the values the model gives to each possible result. They don't guarantee that the answer is correct, and you can't compare them across models, or across questions with different wording. Choose your thresholds by testing on real examples from your application, and test them again when you change the model.

ChoiceAnswer and ScoreAnswer also have getConfidence(), the provider's own estimate of how sure it is about the whole answer. It is null when the provider doesn't report it. Confidence covers what it means and how this project uses it.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
A provider can refuse to answer one question and still answer the others. That question gets a RefusalAnswer, and response.isRefused(name) returns true for it. The typed getters, such as getYesNo(name), throw an IllegalStateException for a refused question. A refusal doesn't make the call fail.

The components in this project never read a refusal as an answer:

Component A refused question DecisionJudge is an ERROR finding: not a pass, but it fails the verdict only with failOnError(true) DecisionGuardrail counts as if the hazard fired, so the turn is refused DecisionChatModel is null in the reply DecisionConsistency is left out of the statistics

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: response.getMetadata() has the token usage of the call. When the provider reports them, it also has the response id and the model that answered.

docs.title: Atomic questions, composed in code
docs.text:
The most important habit is asking several narrow questions instead of one broad one. The providers answer every question of a call against the same input, so a third question costs far less than a third call.

DecisionResponse response = decisionModel.call(DecisionPrompt.builder()
    .input(input)
    .question("helpfulness",  helpfulnessRubric)    // ScoreQuestion
    .question("is_plausible", plausibilityCheck)    // YesNoQuestion
    .question("is_grounded",  groundednessCheck)    // YesNoQuestion
    .build());

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App
    participant Model as DecisionModel
    participant Provider

    App->>Model: call(input, 3 questions)
    Model->>Provider: one request
    Note over Provider: the input is read once, and every<br/>question is answered against it
    Provider-->>Model: one answer per question name
    Model-->>App: DecisionResponse

    App->>App: getScore("helpfulness").getValue() >= 2.0
    App->>App: getYesNo("is_plausible").isYes(0.8)
    App->>App: getYesNo("is_grounded").isYes(0.8)

The payoff is that each answer keeps its own threshold. An answer that is fluent and exactly on topic but quotes an impossible temperature fails on is_plausible alone. A single overall rating would average that problem away into a middling score.

A few more habits give more reliable answers:

  • Pick the kind of question from what your code does next. A yes/no question when the code takes one of two paths, a choice when it takes one of several, a score when it needs a level.
  • Add descriptions when a name alone can be read in more than one way. The whenYes and whenNo criteria do the same for a yes/no question.
  • Send only what the decision needs. A short message, or a few relevant fields, gives clearer answers than a whole customer record or a long conversation.
  • Try your questions on real inputs before you rely on them, including inputs that are hard to decide. If the probabilities stay close to 0.5, or are spread over several options, change the wording and try again.

docs.title: Speculative questions
docs.text:
Since extra questions are cheap, ask ones you might not need. bug_severity only matters if a ticket turns out to be a technical report, but which it is is what the call is working out. Ask both and let your code decide what to read:

switch (response.getChoice("department").getValue()) {
    case "technical" -> handleBug(response.getScore("bug_severity").getValue());
    case "billing"   -> handleBilling(response.getYesNo("refund_requested").getProbability());
    default          -> route(response);
}

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
DecisionOptions holds the settings of a call, such as the model to use. Set it on the prompt to change the model's defaults for one call:

DecisionPrompt prompt = DecisionPrompt.builder()
    .text("Where is my order? I ordered it two weeks ago.")
    .question("topic", ChoiceQuestion.of("What is the message about?",
            "delivery", "product", "account", "other"))
    .options(DecisionOptions.builder().model("d1-omni:2b").build())
    .build();

The components here that call a model take the same options: DecisionJudge.builder(...), DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.builder(...) and DecisionChatModel.builder(...) each have an options(DecisionOptions) method, sent with every call they make.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
The components in this project take a DecisionModel and nothing else, so any Spring AI implementation works. Spring AI ships three. Each has a Spring Boot starter that contributes a DecisionModel bean.

Provider Starter Default model Runs Ollama spring-ai-starter-model-ollama d1-omni:600m on your machine, no API key OpenAI spring-ai-starter-model-openai gpt-6-luna hosted System One spring-ai-starter-model-systemone jev-latest hosted (TypeSafe) or local (Laya, llmman, Ollama)

The Spring AI reference pages linked above are the full description of each. This page covers what matters when you use them with this project.

docs.title: Ollama
docs.text:
The quickest way to start. Install Ollama 0.40.4 or later, pull the default decision model, and add the starter:

ollama pull d1-omni:600m

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-model-ollama</artifactId>
</dependency>

# application.properties; all optional
spring.ai.ollama.base-url=http://localhost:11434
spring.ai.ollama.decision.model=d1-omni:600m
spring.ai.ollama.init.pull-model-strategy=when_missing

Small models lean on descriptions

Small decision models, such as d1-omni:600m, depend a lot on the descriptions of the options and levels. Write the whenYes/whenNo criteria and the option descriptions out, rather than relying on a name alone.

docs.title: OpenAI
docs.text:
OpenAiDecisionModel uses the OpenAI Decisions API, an endpoint separate from chat completions.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-model-openai</artifactId>
</dependency>

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}
spring.ai.openai.decision.model=gpt-6-luna

OpenAI is the one provider that can refuse a single question and still answer the others. See how each component treats a refusal.

docs.title: System One
docs.text:
System One is the POST /v1/systemone protocol of the decision models of TypeSafe. Laya, llmman and Ollama serve it too, so one implementation works with all four.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-model-systemone</artifactId>
</dependency>

spring.ai.systemone.api-key=${TYPESAFE_API_KEY}
# For a local server instead of TypeSafe:
# spring.ai.systemone.base-url=http://localhost:8002
# spring.ai.systemone.decision.model=english

docs.title: What each supports
docs.text:
Feature Ollama OpenAI System One Text input Yes Yes Yes Text with images No Yes, inline images only No Fields input Yes Yes Yes Conversation input Yes Yes Yes Probabilities Yes Yes Yes Confidence (choice, score) Yes Yes Yes Refusals No Yes No Response id No Yes TypeSafe only

Three of these matter for the components here:

  • Fields input is what they send. The judge, the guardrail and the chat adapter all build a FieldsInput, which every provider supports.
  • A confidence of 0 can mean "none reported". With Ollama and System One, the client reports 0 when the server sends no confidence. The confidence gate escalates such an answer, which is the safe reading.
  • Text only, except OpenAI. An image in the input makes the call fail on Ollama and System One. DecisionChatModel's default input rejects media for that reason.

docs.title: More than one decision model
docs.text:
When two provider starters are on the classpath, each auto-configures its own decision model. Choose one with spring.ai.model.decision:

# ollama, openai, systemone or none
spring.ai.model.decision=ollama

Or build the models yourself and give each component the one it should use. A common split is a small local model for the guardrail, which runs on every turn, and a larger one for the judge:

DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.builder(localDecisionModel).build();
DecisionJudge.builder(hostedDecisionModel).build();

A component can also use a different model of the same provider through its options(...):

DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .options(DecisionOptions.builder().model("d1-omni:2b").build())
    .build();

docs.title: Thresholds do not carry over
docs.text: The providers use different models, so their probabilities differ. A threshold tuned on one model is not valid on another. When you change the provider or the model, check your thresholds again; DecisionConsistency shows which of them sit on unstable answers.

docs.title: Failures and retries
docs.text:
The DecisionModel API has no common exception for an outage. Each provider throws its own, after its own retries: the System One client, for example, retries connection failures, timeouts, rate limits and server errors before it throws a SystemOneException.

The self-refine advisor needs to tell an outage from a misconfiguration, and takes a predicate for it. For a System One or Ollama model, add the provider's own test to the default:

DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder()
    .judge(judge)
    .transientErrorPredicate(((Predicate<Throwable>) DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor::isTransient)
            .or(SystemOneRetryUtils::isTransient))
    .build();

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Spring AI observes decision model calls like the calls of other models: a gen_ai.client.operation observation with the decision operation name and the provider as gen_ai.system. Every call a judge or a guardrail makes is recorded that way, with no configuration here. See Decision Model observability in the Spring AI reference.

docs.title: DecisionGuardrailAdvisor
docs.text:
Screens what the user sends and what the model answers, refusing the turn when either crosses a line.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-guardrail</artifactId>
</dependency>

Features:

  • Separate input and output hazard batteries
  • One call per screened text, whatever the number of hazards
  • Four outcomes: PASS, REVIEW, BLOCK, SUPPORT
  • A blocked input never reaches the model at all
  • A severity rubric that can promote a borderline case to a refusal
  • A hazard the model refuses to answer is never read as safe
  • A refusal is marked as a Spring AI GuardrailRefusal, so entity(...) throws rather than parsing it
  • Streaming, with the reply held back until it is screened

docs.title: Why both directions
docs.text: They fail differently. An input battery catches the request that should never have been made. An output battery catches the reply that should never have been given, and it is the only one of the two that notices a jailbreak that actually worked, because a successful one looks innocuous going in.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The two directions belong in different places of the advisor chain, so the recommended setup is one advisor per direction:

ChatClient chatClient = ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
    .defaultAdvisors(
            DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.input(decisionModel),
            MessageChatMemoryAdvisor.builder(chatMemory).build(),
            DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.output(decisionModel))
    .build();

input(...) screens the user message with DecisionGuardrail.defaultInputBattery(), and output(...) screens the reply with defaultOutputBattery(). Together they cover jailbreak attempts, physical harm, illegal help and self-harm signals.

MessageChatMemoryAdvisor stands for whatever keeps the conversation. Spring AI 2.1 deprecates it in favour of the session advisors, and the placement is the same with those; see where it sits.

For a chain with no chat memory and no advisor that rewrites the user message, a single advisor that screens both directions is enough:

ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
    .defaultAdvisors(DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.builder(decisionModel).build())
    .build();

See where it sits for what separates the two setups.

docs.title: How a turn flows
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Caller
    participant I as Input advisor
    participant O as Output advisor
    participant D as DecisionModel
    participant M as Chat model

    C->>I: prompt(userMessage)
    I->>D: input battery, one call
    D-->>I: Verdict

    alt BLOCK or SUPPORT
        I-->>C: refusal, model not called
    else PASS or REVIEW
        I->>O: nextCall(request)
        O->>M: nextCall(request)
        M-->>O: answer
        O->>D: output battery, one call
        D-->>O: Verdict
        alt BLOCK or SUPPORT
            O-->>C: refusal replaces the answer
        else PASS or REVIEW
            O-->>C: answer
        end
    end

Two things to read off this. A blocked input returns before nextCall, so the model is never invoked and nothing is generated or spent. And a battery screens a text in one decision call carrying all of its hazards plus the severity rubric, so a battery of six hazards costs what one would. A reply that holds several texts, such as a thinking block ahead of the answer, takes one call for each; see where it sits.

A REVIEW outcome passes through and is logged rather than refused. It exists so a borderline turn reaches a human instead of being decided by a threshold. Setting blockOnReview(true) collapses that branch into the refusal path.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Outcome Meaning Advisor behaviour PASS nothing crossed a threshold the turn proceeds REVIEW borderline; worth a human looking proceeds, logged (unless blockOnReview) BLOCK refuse the turn the refusal replaces the answer SUPPORT refuse, and route to help the support message replaces the answer

They are ordered by precedence: when several hazards fire, the most serious one wins.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
Two thresholds give three postures:

Probability Posture above actionThreshold (0.70) the hazard's configured action applies above reviewThreshold (0.35) flagged for a human rather than decided by a number below both passes

A separate severity rubric (levels 0 to 3) promotes a review to a refusal at severityBlockThreshold (2.0): a borderline probability about something serious is not a borderline problem.

docs.title: A hazard keeps its own action
docs.text:
A hazard that fires or is flagged refuses the turn with its own action, and never less than a BLOCK. A hazard the model refuses to answer is a plain BLOCK, since a refusal is no evidence of that hazard in particular:

How the hazard refuses the turn The turn is refused with it fires, above actionThreshold its action it is flagged, and the severity rubric promotes it its action, at least BLOCK it is flagged, and the advisor refuses on review (blockOnReview) its action, at least BLOCK the model refuses to answer it BLOCK

A flagged hazard keeps its action also next to a hazard that blocks: a block must not hide a call for support.

In the blockOnReview case the verdict's outcome stays REVIEW, while the response context reports the outcome the turn was refused with. DecisionGuardrail.refusalOutcome(verdict) gives that outcome, for a caller that applies the same rule itself; for a verdict that passes it returns PASS.

So a self-harm signal still routes to SUPPORT, with the support message, when it is only borderline but serious. And a hazard whose action is only REVIEW still blocks the turn when the model would not answer it.

docs.title: Refusals fail closed
docs.text: A provider can refuse to answer a single question. A hazard the model refuses to answer is not taken as absent: a refusal to look at a text is no evidence that the text is safe. It blocks the turn, and is listed in Verdict.refused() and in the summary as hazard (refused); a flagged hazard appears there as hazard (flagged). The same holds for the severity rubric: a borderline hazard whose seriousness the model would not rate is refused.

    class DecisionGuardrail {
        +String TEXT_FIELD$
        +String SEVERITY_QUESTION$
        +screen(DecisionModel, String) Verdict
        +questions() Map
        +evaluate(DecisionResponse) Verdict
        +refusalOutcome(Verdict) Outcome
        +defaultInputBattery()$ DecisionGuardrail
        +defaultOutputBattery()$ DecisionGuardrail
    }

    class Hazard {
        <<record>>
        +YesNoQuestion question
        +Outcome action
    }

    class Verdict {
        <<record>>
        +Outcome outcome
        +List~String~ triggered
        +List~String~ flagged
        +List~String~ refused
        +double severity
        +Map~String, Double~ scores
        +blocked() boolean
        +summary() String
    }

    class Outcome {
        <<enumeration>>
        PASS
        REVIEW
        BLOCK
        SUPPORT
    }

    DecisionGuardrailAdvisor --> "1..2" DecisionGuardrail : input and output
    DecisionGuardrail "1" *-- "1..*" Hazard : one question each
    DecisionGuardrail ..> Verdict : screen() produces
    Hazard --> Outcome : what firing means
    Verdict --> Outcome : the worst that fired

Hazard, Verdict and Outcome are nested in DecisionGuardrail. The cardinality on the first edge is the part worth noticing: either battery may be null, which is how you screen one direction only. Not both, since an advisor that screens neither does nothing and the builder rejects it; hence one or two.

Unlike DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor, this advisor does not take a DecisionJudge. A battery prescribes its own questions and thresholds, because a guardrail policy is a fixed thing rather than something supplied per call. screen(...) performs the decision call; evaluate(...) applies the thresholds to a response you already have, which is what makes the policy testable without a model.

DecisionGuardrail does not need ChatClient. Outside a chat, call screen(...) yourself:

DecisionGuardrail.Verdict verdict = DecisionGuardrail.defaultInputBattery()
        .screen(decisionModel, uploadedText);

if (verdict.blocked()) {
    reject(verdict.summary());   // e.g. block [jailbreak]
}

docs.title: Builder Configuration
docs.text:
DecisionGuardrailAdvisor advisor = DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.builder(decisionModel)
    .options(DecisionOptions.builder().model("d1-omni:600m").build())
    .inputBattery(DecisionGuardrail.defaultInputBattery())
    .outputBattery(DecisionGuardrail.defaultOutputBattery())
    .refusal("I can't help with that.")
    .blockOnReview(false)
    .order(DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.DEFAULT_ORDER)
    .build();
Builder method Default Description options(DecisionOptions) the model's defaults Options sent with every screening call, such as the model name. inputBattery(DecisionGuardrail) defaultInputBattery() null skips input screening. outputBattery(DecisionGuardrail) defaultOutputBattery() null skips output screening. refusal(String) "I can't help with that." Returned on a BLOCK. supportMessage(String) a signposting message Returned on a SUPPORT. blockOnReview(boolean) false Refuse a flagged turn, with the wording of what was flagged. order(int) DEFAULT_ORDER (LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1000) Where in the chain this runs. See where it sits. scheduler(Scheduler) BaseAdvisor.DEFAULT_SCHEDULER Runs the screening calls when streaming, since they block.

At least one battery must be set.

The two factories are shorthands for the builder:

Factory Is DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.input(model) builder(model).outputBattery(null).order(BEFORE_MEMORY_ORDER).build() DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.output(model) builder(model).inputBattery(null).build()

Use the builder form when you need a custom battery, wording or options for one direction.

docs.title: Where it sits
docs.text:
A higher order value runs later on the way in, nearer the model, and so inside every advisor with a lower value. The request is best screened at the outer edge of the chain and the reply at the inner one.

Position Order What it gives BEFORE_MEMORY_ORDER, used by input(...) HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 100 Ahead of chat memory (+ 200), the tool loop (+ 300), retrieval (0) and the self-refine advisor DEFAULT_ORDER, used by output(...) and the builder LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1000 Nearer the model than all of those

The input advisor, before memory:

  • screens what the person wrote, before a retrieval advisor inlines documents into the message or the self-refine advisor appends its feedback. Either can trip a hazard the person never raised, or bury one they did;
  • runs once per turn, however many retries or tool calls follow;
  • a blocked message is never stored in chat memory, so it cannot come back as history on the next turn, where only the new message is screened.

The output advisor, next to the model:

  • screens every reply the model produces: each retry attempt before it is judged, and any text alongside a tool call. A reply that is only a tool call has no text and is skipped, and tool results are not screened; see what is not screened;
  • what chat memory stores is the refusal, not the reply it replaced.

A reply can hold several texts: the answer and the reasoning (thinking) of a choice, a Gemini answer split into parts, or several choices when the model is asked for more than one. The output battery screens the answer and the reasoning of each choice on their own, one call each, and refuses the reply when any of them is blocked. Screening them apart keeps a long harmless text from diluting a short harmful one. The reasoning is screened because the caller can read it: it is part of the message, and of the stream. The price: a safe answer can be refused because its reasoning dwelt on a hazard.

The same holds with Spring AI's session advisors (SessionAdvisors), which replace MessageChatMemoryAdvisor from 2.1 on: BEFORE_MEMORY_ORDER is ahead of the session turn advisor (HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 200), and DEFAULT_ORDER is nearer the model than the session memory advisor (HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 1000).

A single advisor screens the input in the inner position

DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.builder(model).build() screens both directions at DEFAULT_ORDER. With chat memory or a message-rewriting advisor in the chain, its input battery then sees the rewritten message rather than the person's, and a blocked message is already in memory by the time it is refused. Use the two factories there.

Either way a refusal is final. The refused response carries DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.OUTCOME_CONTEXT_KEY in its context, holding the outcome's name, and the self-refine advisor's default skipEvaluationPredicate neither judges nor retries it.

docs.title: What is not screened
docs.text:
The advisor screens text that a person wrote and text that the model answered. It does not screen what tools exchange with the model:

  • the arguments of a tool call that the model asks for;
  • the result of a tool, which the model reads on the next round of the tool calling loop. A round of the loop does not screen the user message again either, since it was screened when the turn started;
  • a tool result that is returned directly as the reply (returnDirect), because the tool calling loop builds that reply outside the advisor.

Treat the result of a tool that reads external content, such as a web page, a document or an email, as untrusted input, and guard it in the tool.

docs.title: What a refusal looks like
docs.text:
A refusal is an ordinary reply: one generation whose text is the refusal or the support message. Two markers tell it from an answer of the model:

  • the context of the response holds DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.OUTCOME_CONTEXT_KEY, with the outcome the turn was refused with, BLOCK or SUPPORT;
  • the generation is a Spring AI GuardrailRefusal: its finish reason is GuardrailRefusal.FINISH_REASON, in the FILTERED finish reason category, and GuardrailRefusal.isRefusal(chatResponse) is true.

A refusal that replaces a reply keeps the id, the model, the token usage and the rate limit of that reply, because the reply was generated and paid for. It keeps no other metadata, because a chat model can store the reply itself there, for example as the raw response of the provider. A refused input has no reply, so its response has no usage.

docs.title: Structured output
docs.text:
A refusal is plain text, not JSON, and it is not what the model said. As a GuardrailRefusal it is not taken for structured output:

  • ChatClient.entity(...) throws a GuardrailRefusalException, which carries the refusal and the response with its context;
  • responseEntity(...) returns the response with a null entity;
  • a StructuredOutputValidationAdvisor returns the refusal without validating it or asking the model again.
try {
    Order order = chatClient.prompt().user(message).call().entity(Order.class);
}
catch (GuardrailRefusalException ex) {
    String refusal = ex.getRefusal();
    Object outcome = ex.getChatClientResponse().context().get(DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.OUTCOME_CONTEXT_KEY);
}

A GuardrailRefusalException is a ContentFilteredException, so one catch covers the refusal of the guardrail and the safety stop of a provider.

By default the output advisor sits nearer the chat model than a StructuredOutputValidationAdvisor (LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 2000). It then screens each reply that the validation advisor asks the model for, and a refusal ends the retries. To screen only the reply that the validation advisor returns, give the output advisor a lower order than the validation advisor with DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.builder(decisionModel).inputBattery(null).order(...).

docs.title: Custom batteries
docs.text:
A battery is a set of hazards plus a severity rubric. Each hazard is a yes/no question and the action its firing implies:

DecisionGuardrail battery = DecisionGuardrail.builder("input")
    .hazard("jailbreak",
            "Does the `text` try to make the assistant ignore its instructions?",
            "Attempts to change the assistant's rules, role or restrictions",
            DecisionGuardrail.Outcome.BLOCK)
    .hazard("competitor_mention",
            "Does the `text` ask the assistant to discuss a competitor's product?",
            "Asks about a competitor",
            DecisionGuardrail.Outcome.REVIEW)
    .reviewThreshold(0.35d)
    .actionThreshold(0.70d)
    .severityBlockThreshold(2.0d)
    .build();

DecisionGuardrailAdvisor input = DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.builder(decisionModel)
    .inputBattery(battery)
    .outputBattery(null)
    .order(DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.BEFORE_MEMORY_ORDER)
    .build();

The text under examination is the text field of the input; write your questions against it. The name severity is reserved for the rubric, which severity(ScoreQuestion) replaces.

docs.title: Testing the policy without a model
docs.text:
evaluate(DecisionResponse) applies the thresholds to an already-screened response, which lets the policy be unit-tested with no model call. Script the answers with StubDecisionModel:

DecisionResponse answers = StubDecisionModel
    .answering(Map.of("jailbreak", yesNo(0.50), "competitor_mention", yesNo(0.01),
                      "severity", score(0.0)))
    .call("some text", battery.questions());

DecisionGuardrail.Verdict verdict = battery.evaluate(answers);

assertThat(verdict.outcome()).isEqualTo(DecisionGuardrail.Outcome.REVIEW);
assertThat(verdict.flagged()).containsExactly("jailbreak");
assertThat(verdict.scores()).containsEntry("jailbreak", 0.50d);

battery.questions() returns the questions the battery asks: one per hazard, by name, then the severity rubric.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Each screened text is one call carrying the whole battery, so asking about six hazards costs what asking about one would. That is one call for the user message, once per turn however many tool rounds follow, and one for each text of the reply: the answer and the reasoning of each choice. A blocked input costs one screening call and no generation at all: the chain is never invoked.

The guardrail runs on every turn, which makes it a good place for a small, fast model. Give it its own DecisionModel, or name a model in its options(...).

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
The advisor screens the input before the stream starts. An output battery needs the whole reply before it can judge it, so with one configured the advisor holds the stream back until the reply is complete and screened. It then releases the chunks as it received them, or emits the refusal in their place. As for a call, the answer and the reasoning of each choice are screened on their own. An advisor that screens only the input does not delay the stream.

The call to the decision model blocks, so when streaming it runs on a scheduler, BaseAdvisor.DEFAULT_SCHEDULER unless scheduler(...) sets another.

docs.title: DecisionEvaluator
docs.text:
A DecisionJudge behind Spring AI's Evaluator interface, so a decision model drops into code already written against the framework's evaluation SPI.

It ships in spring-ai-decision-judge, next to the judge.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Spring AI's org.springframework.ai.evaluation.Evaluator is a one-method interface:

EvaluationResponse evaluate(EvaluationRequest request);

Its two shipped implementations, RelevancyEvaluator and FactCheckingEvaluator, prompt a chat model and parse a verdict out of the prose. DecisionEvaluator implements the same interface with typed questions instead, so anything holding an Evaluator gets a stricter one without changing a line.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Evaluator evaluator = new DecisionEvaluator(judge);

EvaluationResponse result = evaluator.evaluate(
        new EvaluationRequest(userQuestion, retrievedDocuments, assistantAnswer));

if (!result.isPass()) {
    log.warn("{} (score {})", result.getFeedback(), result.getScore());
}

docs.title: The mapping
docs.text:
EvaluationRequest Judged input field getUserText() user_question getResponseContent() assistant_answer getDataList() supporting_context, one entry per document with text (only when non-empty) EvaluationResponse From isPass() verdict.passed() getScore() the fraction of the criteria that applied which passed; NOT_APPLICABLE ones are left out getFeedback() verdict.feedback() getMetadata() the full DecisionVerdict and a per-criterion outcome map 
DecisionVerdict verdict = (DecisionVerdict) result.getMetadata().get(DecisionEvaluator.VERDICT_METADATA_KEY);
Map<String, String> findings =
        (Map<String, String>) result.getMetadata().get(DecisionEvaluator.FINDINGS_METADATA_KEY);
// {helpfulness=PASSED, is_plausible=FAILED}

The single score is lossy on purpose

EvaluationResponse has room for one float, while a judge holds one threshold per criterion. The score is the fraction of the applicable criteria that passed, and the per-criterion detail is preserved in the metadata. If that view is what you are after, call DecisionJudge.judge directly and read the DecisionVerdict.

An inconclusive criterion counts as neither passed nor failed, so it lowers the score without being treated as a failure, the same stance DecisionVerdict.passed() takes.

docs.title: Supporting documents
docs.text:
getDataList() carries the retrieved Documents, which is the evidence a groundedness criterion needs. Their texts reach the input as the supporting_context list, one entry per document, so write such a criterion against that field:

DecisionJudge grounded = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .yesNo("is_grounded", YesNoQuestion.builder()
        .text("Is every claim in `assistant_answer` supported by `supporting_context`?")
        .whenNo("Introduces facts the context does not support")
        .build(), 0.7d)
    .build();

To skip that criterion when a request carries no documents, make it conditional:

DecisionCriterion.yesNo("is_grounded", groundedQuestion, 0.7d)
    .appliesWhen(input -> !input.context().isEmpty())

This is also how a groundedness check gets real evidence in a RAG setting. The self-refine advisor sees the retrieved context only inside user_question, and only at its default order.

docs.title: DecisionJudge
docs.text:
A model-as-a-judge built out of atomic questions rather than one rubric prompt. Every criterion is answered against the same input in a single call, and each keeps its own threshold.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-judge</artifactId>
</dependency>

The judge needs only the DecisionModel API, so it can be used in a test suite or a batch evaluation without ChatClient.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
A judge holds a list of criteria. Most are a question plus what counts as passing it:

  • a yes/no question passes when its probability of yes reaches a minimum
  • a score passes when at least half of its probability is on the levels at or above your minimum
  • a choice passes when at least half of its probability is on the options you accept

See how a verdict is decided for the details.

The rest are code checks: plain Java predicates for anything the input already settles, such as whether a tool was called. They never reach the model.

judge(...) sends every question in one request and returns a DecisionVerdict: whether everything passed, a finding per criterion, the raw response, and feedback synthesised from the criteria that did not.

docs.text:
A judge is built from criteria, and each criterion pairs a question with its own pass condition:
