The shape to take from this: a judge is a list of criteria and nothing else. It holds a DecisionModel and spends at most one call per judge(...), whatever the number of criteria. It makes none when no question applies, or when failFast skips it. Code checks run locally and add nothing to that.

docs.title: How the judge, the advisor and the evaluator fit together
docs.text:
These three are a hub and two spokes, not a chain. DecisionJudge is the engine; the other two are independent adapters that put it behind a Spring AI extension point. Neither spoke uses the other.

flowchart TB
    J["DecisionJudge<br/><small>criteria in, verdict out</small>"]
    S["DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor<br/><small>CallAdvisor</small>"]
    E["DecisionEvaluator<br/><small>Spring AI Evaluator SPI</small>"]
    S --> J
    E --> J
Type Use it when DecisionJudge (this page) you want a verdict in your own code, with the per-criterion findings DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor a ChatClient should judge its own answer and retry when it falls short DecisionGuardrailAdvisor a turn should be refused rather than retried: an unsafe answer is not a draft DecisionEvaluator existing code is written against Spring AI's Evaluator, and you want a decision model behind it

DecisionGuardrailAdvisor is the odd one out: it builds its own hazard batteries rather than taking a DecisionJudge, because the questions and thresholds are prescribed by the guardrail policy rather than supplied per use.

docs.title: Why not just ask a chat model
docs.text:
Spring AI ships RelevancyEvaluator and FactCheckingEvaluator. Both prompt a second chat model and read a yes or a no out of its reply. That fails in two directions. The model may answer in a form the parser does not expect, and one yes-or-no cannot say which of several things was wrong. A judge built from typed questions cannot come back malformed, and keeps the dimensions separate.

A judge model DecisionJudge Verdict prose to parse typed answers Dimensions one overall rating one threshold per criterion Cost of a third check a third prompt, or a longer one negligible: same call Feedback generated, varies run to run synthesised from your own rubric Undecided indistinguishable from failed reported as INCONCLUSIVE Could not judge indistinguishable from failed reported as ERROR

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
DecisionJudge judge = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .score("helpfulness", ScoreQuestion.builder()
        .text("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
        .level("Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic")
        .level("Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point")
        .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps remain")
        .level("Excellent: fully and correctly addressed")
        .build(), 2.0d)
    .yesNo("is_plausible", YesNoQuestion.builder()
        .text("Are the numeric values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
        .whenNo("At least one value is impossible")
        .build(), 0.7d)
    .build();

DecisionVerdict verdict = judge.judge(question, answer);

if (!verdict.passed()) {
    System.out.println(verdict.feedback());
}

docs.title: The input a judge builds
docs.text:
judge(String question, String answer) builds a two-field input:

{ "user_question": "...", "assistant_answer": "..." }

When there is more to judge against, build a DecisionJudgeInput. Its fields become the input under fixed names, the same wherever a judge is used, so write your questions against them:

Builder method Input field Shape question(String) user_question string answer(String) assistant_answer string expected(Object) expected_output a string, number, boolean, map or list: the reference to judge against context(String) / context(List<String>) supporting_context list, one entry per document toolCall(ToolCall) / toolCalls(List<ToolCall>) tool_calls list of {name, arguments, result} field(String, Object) the name you give anything else 
DecisionVerdict verdict = judge.judge(DecisionJudgeInput.builder()
        .question("Will I need an umbrella in Dublin tomorrow?")
        .answer(answer)
        .expected("Rain is likely; bring an umbrella.")
        .field("search_required", true)
        .toolCalls(toolCalls)
        .build());

Empty context and tool-call lists are left out rather than sent as empty lists, so a criterion can tell "no evidence" from "evidence that says nothing". The constants live on DecisionJudgeInput (QUESTION_FIELD, EXPECTED_FIELD, TOOL_CALLS_FIELD, ...).

A value the model input cannot carry, such as an arbitrary object, is rejected when the input is built, with a message naming the field.

For anything that is not a question-and-answer pair, pass the input yourself. Any DecisionInput works: fields, a plain text or a conversation.

DecisionVerdict verdict = judge.judge(DecisionInput.fields(Map.of(
        "passage", retrievedText,
        "claim",   claimUnderTest)));

docs.title: Code criteria
docs.text:
Some criteria need no model, because the answer is already in the input: whether the agent searched when it had to, whether the answer parses, whether it matches the expected output exactly. Declare those as checks:

DecisionJudge judge = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .check("matches_search_expectation",
           input -> !input.toolCalls().isEmpty()
                   == Boolean.TRUE.equals(input.field("search_required", Boolean.class)),
           "searched when no search was required, or skipped a required search")
    .yesNo("is_grounded", groundedQuestion, 0.7d)
    .build();

A check is a Predicate<DecisionJudgeInput> plus the defect to report when it returns false.

  • It never reaches the model. Checks run locally before the call. Only the questions are sent, still in one request.
  • It lands in the same verdict. A failed check is a FAILED finding: it fails the verdict, its defect goes into the feedback and it shows in summary(). Its answer is null, since there is no model answer.
  • A check that throws is a bug, not a verdict. The exception propagates out of judge(...) before any request is made.
  • A judge needs at least one question. A judge of checks alone would be a plain predicate.

judge(DecisionInput) works with checks too, as long as the input is a fields input: they read it through DecisionJudgeInput.of(fieldsInput) and its field(name, type) reader. A text or conversation input with code checks is rejected with an IllegalArgumentException.

Do not ask a model a question code can answer

A question that a one-line comparison settles exactly is better as a check. It is free, it is never wrong, and it removes a source of variance from the verdict.

docs.title: Builder Configuration
docs.text:
Builder method Default Description options(DecisionOptions) the model's defaults Options sent with every judging call, such as the model name. yesNo(String, YesNoQuestion, double) — A criterion passing when the probability of yes is at or above the minimum. score(String, ScoreQuestion, double) — A criterion passing when at least half its probability is on the levels at or above the minimum. choice(String, ChoiceQuestion, String...) — A criterion passing when at least half its probability is on the accepted options. Validates that the options exist on the choice. check(String, Predicate<DecisionJudgeInput>, String) — A code check: passes when the predicate returns true, otherwise reports the defect. criterion(DecisionCriterion) — Add a pre-built criterion of either kind. minConfidence(double) 0.6 How much of a choice's or score's probability must support its verdict; below it, INCONCLUSIVE. See undecided, not failed. Yes/no criteria are unaffected. failOnInconclusive(boolean) false Treat an undecided criterion as a failure. failOnError(boolean) false Treat a criterion the model refused to answer (ERROR) as a failure. failFast(boolean) false When a code check fails, skip the model call; the questions become NOT_APPLICABLE. feedbackRenderer(Function<List<DecisionFinding>, String>) DecisionJudge::defaultFeedback Replace the wording fed back to the model.

Criterion names must be unique across both kinds, and a judge needs at least one question criterion. A score's minimum above the top of its rubric is rejected when the judge is built.

docs.title: Criteria that only sometimes apply
docs.text:
A question can be made conditional with appliesWhen. When the predicate returns false the question is not sent, and its finding is NOT_APPLICABLE: it neither passes nor fails. A groundedness check on a turn with no retrieved context is the typical case:

DecisionJudge judge = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .criterion(DecisionCriterion.yesNo("is_grounded", groundedQuestion, 0.7d)
        .appliesWhen(input -> !input.context().isEmpty()))
    .yesNo("is_relevant", relevantQuestion, 0.7d)
    .build();

When no question applies, no call is made and verdict.response() is null.

docs.title: Criteria that depend on other answers
docs.text:
Rubrics branch. An answer that asks which Springfield is meant should not be marked down for leaving out the forecast's timing. whenChosen and whenPassed make a question depend on another criterion's outcome:

DecisionJudge judge = DecisionJudge.builder(decisionModel)
    .choice("mode", ChoiceQuestion.builder()
        .text("How does `assistant_answer` respond to `user_question`?")
        .option("answered", "Gives the weather")
        .option("clarification_needed", "Asks which place is meant")
        .build(), "answered", "clarification_needed")
    .criterion(DecisionCriterion.yesNo("has_details", detailsQuestion, 0.7d)
        .whenChosen("mode", "answered"))
    .build();
  • The branch costs nothing. Every question is answered in the one call, so has_details is asked anyway, and the dependency is resolved in Java afterwards. Judge frameworks built on chat models walk such a graph one model call per node.
  • The branch follows the probability, not just the top option. It is taken when at least half of the choice's probability, and at least minConfidence, is on the options whenChosen names. A choice split 0.51 to 0.49 selects nothing.
  • When the choice lands elsewhere or doesn't settle, the dependent is NOT_APPLICABLE, with a detail such as has_details: does not apply, mode was "clarification_needed". It neither passes nor fails.
  • An undecided dependency (INCONCLUSIVE, ERROR or NOT_APPLICABLE) makes its dependents NOT_APPLICABLE too: nothing was selected for them to rely on.
  • whenPassed("name") depends on a criterion having passed. That criterion can be a code check.
  • A dependency must be declared before its dependents, which rules out cycles. A whenChosen option must be one of the choice's options. Both are checked when the judge is built.

appliesWhen and a dependency combine. appliesWhen is judged on the input before the call, and a false result means the question is not sent at all. The dependency is judged on the findings after the call.

docs.text:

        <<sealed interface>>
    }

    DecisionVerdict "1" *-- "1..*" DecisionFinding : one per criterion
    DecisionFinding --> Outcome : how it landed
    DecisionFinding --> DecisionAnswer : what came back

    note for DecisionAnswer "permits YesNoAnswer, ChoiceAnswer,<br/>ScoreAnswer, RefusalAnswer"

response is the untouched DecisionResponse, so the usage counts and the response id are there when you need them. It is null when no question was asked: every question was not applicable, or failFast skipped the call.

summary() is a one-line view of how every criterion landed:

passed=false [helpfulness=PASSED, is_plausible=FAILED]

Each DecisionFinding carries its criterion, the raw answer, an Outcome, and a detail sentence ready to hand back to a model. The answer is null for a code check, for a criterion that was not asked, and for one set aside because its dependency was not met; what the model said about the last kind is still in verdict.response(). Only FAILED blocks the verdict:

Outcome Meaning Blocks? PASSED the criterion was met no FAILED the criterion was not met yes INCONCLUSIVE too little probability supported the verdict only with failOnInconclusive(true) ERROR the model refused to answer this criterion only with failOnError(true) NOT_APPLICABLE not asked (appliesWhen was false, or failFast skipped the call), or asked but its dependency (whenChosen, whenPassed) was not met, so its answer is set aside no

ERROR and NOT_APPLICABLE findings are left out of the feedback, since neither is a defect the model can fix. failOnInconclusive(true) and failOnError(true) make a finding block by reporting it as FAILED: it then appears in failures() and in the feedback, not in inconclusive() or errors().

verdict.failures().forEach(finding ->
        log.warn("{} failed: {}", finding.name(), finding.detail()));

docs.title: Feedback is synthesised, not generated
docs.text:
A decision model returns numbers, never prose, so the feedback is built from the answer and the rubric you wrote. It is deterministic and more specific than a judge model's commentary:

- helpfulness: rated "Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point" (1.20), needs to reach 2.00
  which is "Mostly helpful: minor gaps remain"
- is_plausible: At least one value is impossible (scored 0.04, needs at least 0.70)

A failed yes/no criterion quotes the question's whenNo text, which is why it pays to write it as a statement about the input.

Two details worth knowing. The level quoted is the one the score's value lands on, not the most probable level: the two can disagree on a spread distribution, and quoting a label that contradicts the number would be worse than useless. And the wording is formatted with Locale.ROOT, so 0.70 does not become 0,70 on a comma-decimal JVM and change what the model reads.

One case reads differently. When most of the probability sits below the required level but a share on the top levels lifts the score's value over it, quoting the value would contradict the verdict, so the feedback names what failed instead:

- helpfulness: 0.65 of the probability is below "Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point",
  the level it needs to reach

docs.title: Low confidence is undecided, not failed
docs.text:
A score or a choice is decided by where its probability lies.

A score passes when at least half of its probability sits on the levels at or above minimum. A choice passes when at least half sits on the accepted options, even if the single most likely option is another one.

Deciding from the probability, rather than from the score's value, is what makes a minimum mean "this level or better". An answer rated at level 2 with 90% of the probability, and at the level below with the other 10%, has a value of 1.9. It passes a minimum of 2 all the same:

level 1: 0.10   level 2: 0.90   → value 1.90, 0.90 at or above level 2 → PASSED

A minimum is a level

The levels of a rubric are whole numbers, so a fractional minimum counts from the next whole level: 1.2 asks for level 2 or better. Prefer whole numbers, which say what they mean.

Whether that verdict can be acted on is not a question of how sure the provider says it is, but of how much of the probability supports the verdict: the share on the passing side when it passes, on the failing side when it fails. When that share is below minConfidence (0.6 by default: a clear majority, where a coin flip is 0.5), the criterion is INCONCLUSIVE, and it does not block unless you set failOnInconclusive(true).

The difference from confidence matters. This distribution over a four-level rubric has a confidence of only 0.51, because it is split between two levels, yet both levels pass a minimum of 2:

level 0: 0.00   level 1: 0.07   level 2: 0.52   level 3: 0.41   → 0.93 supports the pass → PASSED

A split close to even is the undecided case. Here the score would pass, but barely more than half of the probability says so:

level 0: 0.45   level 1: 0.00   level 2: 0.00   level 3: 0.55   → 0.55 supports the pass → INCONCLUSIVE

When the provider reports no probabilities, there is no split to read. The score's value must then be at least the minimum, the selected option must be an accepted one, and the answer's own confidence is used in place of the support. When the provider reports no confidence either, there is nothing to gate on, and the answer is acted on as given.

A criterion the model refuses to answer is reported as ERROR rather than thrown, with the reason the provider gave. A refusal says nothing about the answer under judgement, so it costs you that one criterion, not the whole verdict.

docs.title: Testing with DecisionJudge
docs.text:
A judge is a useful test oracle for an LLM feature. It can check meaning where contains(...) would be brittle, and it answers every criterion in one call. Asserting on verdict.passed() alone, however, fails with Expecting value to be true but was false, which hides which criterion failed. Pass the summary and the feedback as the assertion's description:

DecisionVerdict verdict = judge.judge(question, answer);

assertThat(verdict.passed())
    .as("%s%n%s", verdict.summary(), verdict.feedback())
    .isTrue();

A failure then names the criterion, the score it reached and the score it needed:

[passed=false [helpfulness=PASSED, is_plausible=FAILED]
- is_plausible: At least one value is impossible (scored 0.04, needs at least 0.70)]
Expecting value to be true but was false

The %n puts the feedback on its own lines, under the summary.

Three more habits make these tests trustworthy:

  • Build the test's judge with failOnInconclusive(true) and failOnError(true). By default a verdict passes when nothing failed, which suits a live self-refine loop. In a test it would let a criterion the model never decided pass silently.
  • Assert on the failing criteria when you expect a failure, not just on passed(): assertThat(verdict.failures()).extracting(DecisionFinding::name).containsExactly("is_plausible").
  • Keep tests that call a real model out of an ordinary build. Each judge(...) is one model call. Put them in *IT classes behind a Maven profile, and guard them on the provider's key or server being available.

To test the judge's own wiring (your thresholds, dependencies and code checks) without a model, script the answers with StubDecisionModel.

For a criterion that sits close to its threshold, check how much it moves between runs with DecisionConsistency before you build a test on it.

docs.title: DecisionCompositeScore
docs.text:
Several score dimensions combined into one number with weights you control.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-patterns</artifactId>
</dependency>

For ordering, never for gating

The argument for atomic questions over a single rubric prompt is that independent checks must be thresholded independently. An answer that is fluent and on topic but quotes an impossible temperature has to fail on plausibility alone, and any average hides exactly that.

So do not build a pass/fail decision on a composite. DecisionJudge thresholds each criterion separately and is the right tool for that.

docs.title: What it is genuinely for
docs.text:
Ranking a field of candidates that have all already passed: which five of forty applicants to read first, which support ticket to work next.

There the dimensions are not pass conditions, they are preferences, and the weights are the policy. Keeping them in code means a disappointing ranking is fixed by changing a weight rather than by rewording a question.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
DecisionCompositeScore engineering = DecisionCompositeScore.builder()
    .weight("python_depth",    0.40d)
    .weight("system_design",   0.40d)
    .weight("team_leadership", 0.10d)
    .weight("generalist",      0.10d)
    .build();

candidates.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(c -> -engineering.of(c.response())));

Each weighted name must be a score question the response answers.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
Each dimension is divided by its rubric's own height before weighting, so dimensions with different numbers of levels are comparable. With weights summing to 1, the composite is itself in [0, 1].

The height of a rubric is its number of levels minus one. There are two ways to tell the composite what it is:

Call Reads the height from Use it when of(response) the probabilities the answer reports, one per level the provider reports probabilities of(response, questions) the ScoreQuestion that was asked the provider reports none, or you would rather not depend on it 
double composite = engineering.of(response, questions);

double depth = DecisionCompositeScore.normalise(response.getScore("python_depth"));            // 0.0 – 1.0
double same  = DecisionCompositeScore.normalise(response.getScore("python_depth"), depthRubric);

of(response) throws an IllegalStateException for an answer that reports no probabilities. Returning 0 instead would score every candidate identically, a plausible-looking number that silently collapses the ranking.

docs.title: Same data, different profiles
docs.text:
The point of keeping weights in code is that one set of answers serves several rankings:

DecisionCompositeScore ic = DecisionCompositeScore.builder()
    .weight("python_depth", 0.40d).weight("system_design", 0.40d)
    .weight("team_leadership", 0.10d).weight("generalist", 0.10d).build();

DecisionCompositeScore manager = DecisionCompositeScore.builder()
    .weight("python_depth", 0.15d).weight("system_design", 0.20d)
    .weight("team_leadership", 0.40d).weight("generalist", 0.25d).build();

One call produces the answers; two weightings produce two shortlists.

docs.title: Builder Configuration
docs.text:
Builder method Default Description weight(String, double) — A score question's share of the composite. allowUnnormalisedWeights(boolean) false Permit weights that do not sum to 1, which puts the composite's range somewhere other than [0, 1].

build() rejects weights that do not sum to 1 unless you opt out, because weights that do not sum to one are usually a typo rather than an intention.

docs.title: DecisionConfidenceGate
docs.text:
A reusable routing policy: a universal confidence floor, plus per-action thresholds for actions that cost more when they are wrong.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-patterns</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The answer says what; confidence says whether to act on it unattended. This turns that into three decisions:

Decision Meaning EXECUTE confident enough for this action: act on it CONFIRM above the floor but short of what this action demands: ask the user first ESCALATE below the floor, or no confidence was reported: nobody should act on this automatically

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
DecisionConfidenceGate gate = DecisionConfidenceGate.builder()
    .floor(0.60d)
    .require("transfer_funds", 0.85d)
    .build();

switch (gate.decide(response.getChoice("intent"))) {
    case EXECUTE  -> perform(intent);
    case CONFIRM  -> askTheUserToConfirm(intent);
    case ESCALATE -> handOverToAHuman();
}

decide(ChoiceAnswer) uses the selected option as the action name. decide(String, Double) takes them separately, for when the action is not simply the option:

String action = untroubled ? "auto_close" : "route_to_" + department;
gate.decide(action, response.getChoice("department").getConfidence());

DecisionConfidenceGate.withDefaultFloor() is a gate with the default floor and no per-action requirement.

docs.title: When no confidence is reported
docs.text:
ChoiceAnswer.getConfidence() is null when the provider doesn't report one. Without it there is nothing to grant autonomy on, so the gate escalates.

With Ollama and System One, the client reports a confidence of 0 when the server sends none. That is below any floor above zero, so it escalates too.

docs.title: Builder Configuration
docs.text:
Builder method Default Description floor(double) 0.6 The confidence below which every action escalates. require(String, double) — Demand more for one action than the floor asks of the rest.

build() rejects an action demanding less than the floor. Such an action could never be reached, so it is a configuration mistake rather than a preference.

floor() and requiredFor(action) read the policy back, for logging or for showing a user why a confirmation was asked.

docs.title: Why a class rather than an if
docs.text:
Two reasons. The asymmetry between actions is policy, and policy is easier to review, test and change when it lives in one place than when it is spread across call sites. And the floor is a genuinely separate idea from the per-action requirement: it is the line below which the question did not decide, regardless of what you were going to do with the answer.

Take a support ticket about a failing payment integration. It is genuinely both a billing and a technical matter, so the options do not separate:

department   : technical (confidence 0.44)
=> route_to_technical: too uncertain to act on, sent to a person

The confidence lands below the floor, and the gate sends the ticket to a person rather than guessing, while clearer tickets in the same run clear the floor and are handled automatically.

docs.title: DecisionConsistency
docs.text:
Asks the same questions repeatedly and reports how much the answers move.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-patterns</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A single number tells you where an answer sits; it does not tell you whether it would sit there again. That matters when a value lands near a threshold, because there the difference between acting and not acting can be noise rather than judgement.

Sampling a question a few times and looking at the spread is how you find out which of your thresholds rest on solid ground.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Map<String, Object> fields = Map.of("ticket", "My payouts have been failing for 3 days.");
Map<String, DecisionQuestion> questions = Map.of(
        "urgent", YesNoQuestion.of("Does this convey urgency?"));

DecisionConsistency.Report report = DecisionConsistency.sample(decisionModel, fields, questions, 15);

report.statistics().forEach((name, stats) ->
        System.out.printf("%-20s mean %.3f  sd %.3f  range %.3f%n",
                name, stats.mean(), stats.standardDeviation(), stats.range()));

The overload without a sample count draws DEFAULT_SAMPLES (15). A run needs at least two samples to say anything about spread.

docs.title: The question this answers
docs.text:
// The questions whose samples fall on both sides of the threshold you rely on
List<String> shaky = report.unstableAt(0.70d);

A criterion that straddles its threshold makes a decision that is not reproducible: the same input would be accepted on one run and rejected on the next. Either move the threshold, sharpen the question, or route that case to a human.

public record Statistics(String name, List<Double> values, double mean,
                         double standardDeviation, double min, double max) {
    double range();
    boolean straddles(double threshold);
}

docs.title: How the draws are kept independent
docs.text:
Each sample carries a fresh throwaway uid among its fields (DecisionConsistency.UID_FIELD), which forces independent draws rather than a repeat of one cached computation. The fields are otherwise untouched, and the questions are identical across samples.

Because that field name is reserved, fields that already contain a uid are rejected with an IllegalArgumentException. Pass your own identifier under another name.

The questions staying identical matters: this measures the model's own stability, not the effect of rewording a question. Rephrasing to see whether the answer changes is a different and also useful experiment, but it is not this one.

docs.title: What is summarised
docs.text:
Only yes/no answers and scores, which have a single number to track: the probability of yes, and the score's value. A choice's stability is a question about its whole distribution rather than one value, so it is left out of the statistics. Read report.samples() and inspect each getChoice(name).getProbabilities() yourself if you need it.

A question the model refused in one sample has no value there, so that sample is left out of the question's statistics.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
Samples that fail are collected rather than thrown, so a run still produces statistics over whatever came back:

if (!report.failures().isEmpty()) {
    log.warn("{} of {} samples failed", report.failures().size(),
             report.failures().size() + report.samples().size());
}

Each Failure carries the sample's index and the exception the call failed with. A sample that your own executor rejects, for example a bounded pool that is full, is a Failure too, with the RejectedExecutionException as its cause.

docs.title: Cost and concurrency
docs.text:
Fifteen samples are fifteen model calls, four at a time by default. It is a development-time and CI-time tool: run it when choosing a threshold or when a rubric changes, not on every request.

Sampling controls how the samples are drawn:

DecisionConsistency.sample(decisionModel, fields, questions, 15,
        DecisionConsistency.Sampling.defaults()
            .withConcurrency(8)
            .withOptions(DecisionOptions.builder().model("d1-omni:2b").build()));
Sampling Default Description withConcurrency(int) 4 How many calls may be in flight at once. withExecutor(Executor) a pool of the run's own The executor to run on, for example a virtual-thread executor. A supplied executor is never shut down. withOptions(DecisionOptions) the model's defaults Options sent with every call, such as the model name.

One call at a time for a local model

Some local servers answer one request at a time. Use withConcurrency(1) there, so the samples queue in the client rather than time out on the server.

docs.title: DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor
docs.text:
A self-refine CallAdvisor: it judges every model response with a DecisionJudge and, when the response falls short, feeds the defect back into the prompt and tries again.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-self-refine</artifactId>
</dependency>

It brings the judge with it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Request] --> B[Model]
    B --> C{DecisionJudge}
    C -- passed --> D[Return response]
    C -- failed --> E[Append defect to prompt]
    E --> B
    C -- attempts exhausted --> F[Return best attempt<br/>or throw]

This is the same loop as an LLM-as-a-judge advisor, with the judging step swapped. A judge model has to be prompted, has to generate text and has to be coerced into a schema. A decision model is asked typed questions and answers them directly, so the verdict needs no parsing and cannot come back malformed.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
ChatClient chatClient = ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
    .defaultTools(new WeatherTools())
    .defaultAdvisors(DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder()
            .judge(judge)
            .maxRepeatAttempts(3)
            .build())
    .build();

String answer = chatClient.prompt("What is the weather in Paris?").call().content();

docs.title: Builder Configuration
docs.text:
Builder method Default Description judge(DecisionJudge) — (required) What to evaluate each response against. maxRepeatAttempts(int) 3 Retries after the first attempt. Capped at MAX_REPEAT_ATTEMPTS_LIMIT (100). failOnExhaustedAttempts(boolean) false Throw DecisionSelfRefineFailedException instead of returning the best attempt. skipEvaluationPredicate(BiPredicate<ChatClientRequest, ChatClientResponse>) skips what is not the model's answer When it returns true, the response is returned unjudged. judgeErrorPolicy(JudgeErrorPolicy) FAIL_OPEN What to do when the judging call itself fails. See when judging fails. transientErrorPredicate(Predicate<Throwable>) DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor::isTransient Which judging failures count as an outage rather than a misconfiguration. order(int) DEFAULT_ORDER (LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 2000) Where in the advisor chain this runs; BEFORE_TOOLS_ORDER to re-run tools on a retry. See where it sits.

Retry until it passes is not supported

maxRepeatAttempts is capped deliberately. Each attempt is a model call plus a judging call, and a criterion the model cannot satisfy would otherwise loop forever.

docs.title: What the judge can see
docs.text:
The advisor builds a DecisionJudgeInput from the original request and the answer it produced:

Field Carries user_question the system message and the user and assistant turns, each prefixed with its role assistant_answer the final answer tool_calls the tool calls with their results, {name, arguments, result}: read from the prompt at the default order, recorded during the attempt at BEFORE_TOOLS_ORDER (see where it sits)

The input is built from the original request, not the one carrying feedback, so the judge never sees its own previous feedback as part of the question.

supporting_context and expected_output are not filled: the advisor has no retrieved documents or reference answer to put there. Context a retrieval advisor added to the prompt arrives inside user_question. So a criterion that reads supporting_context, or an appliesWhen on input.context(), sees nothing under this advisor; write groundedness against user_question or tool_calls instead.

Read from the prompt, a ToolResponseMessage carries no text of its own, so its results are unpacked into tool_calls rather than dropped. Each result goes to the earliest open call with the same id, or with the same tool name when the provider leaves ids blank, so parallel calls and ids reused across turns stay apart. Tool calls of earlier turns still in the prompt are included too. Write a groundedness criterion against that field:

.yesNo("is_grounded", YesNoQuestion.builder()
    .text("Is every value in `assistant_answer` supported by a result in `tool_calls`?")
    .whenNo("States a value no tool returned")
    .build(), 0.7d)

Whether a tool was called at all is better settled by a code check than asked of the model.

A response can hold several generations: thinking blocks, an answer split into parts, or several choices. The judged answer is the text of the first choice, with thinking left out and its parts joined.

docs.title: What a retry is told
docs.text:
A retry's user message is the original one, followed by:

  1. the reasons the last answer was rejected, in the judge's own wording;
  2. the reasons earlier answers were rejected that the last one no longer shows, so a retry does not fix one defect by bringing another back;
  3. the rejected answer itself, so the model corrects what it wrote rather than starting blind.
What is the weather in Paris?

Your previous answer was rejected by an automated evaluation for these reasons:
- helpfulness: rated "Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic" (0.00), needs to reach 2.00 which is "Mostly helpful: minor gaps remain"

Answers before it were rejected for these reasons, which must not come back:
- is_plausible: Contains an impossible or absurd value (scored 0.03, needs at least 0.70)

This is the answer that was rejected:
<rejected_answer>
No idea.
</rejected_answer>

Answer again, correcting every point above.

The message is rebuilt from the original request each time, and only the latest rejected answer is quoted, so the prompt does not grow with every attempt. Everything stays in the one user message: an advisor further in that reads the last user message, such as retrieval, still finds the question there.

docs.title: What is not judged
docs.text:
A response that is not the model's answer is returned as it is. The default skipEvaluationPredicate covers five cases:

Response Why it is not judged a tool call It is not an answer yet. the output of a returnDirect tool It is the tool's output, and a retry would re-run a tool that may have side effects. the notice of an exceeded tool-call limit It is the tool loop's message; every retry would run the tools into the same limit again. a turn a guardrail refused, such as the guardrail or Spring AI's SafeGuardAdvisor It is the guardrail's wording, and the guardrail would refuse again. Any reply marked as a GuardrailRefusal counts. an answer the provider filtered (FinishReasonCategory.FILTERED) A safety filter stopped it or the model refused, and asking again is filtered again.

A custom predicate replaces that default, so keep these checks if you write your own.

docs.title: Where it sits, and why
docs.text:
The advisor's position in the chain decides what the judge sees and what a retry can fix. ChatClient runs the tool loop in a ToolCallingAdvisor it registers itself, at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 300. A chat memory advisor, when the application adds one, runs at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 200 by default. Retrieval (RetrievalAugmentationAdvisor) and most application advisors run at order 0.

Order The judge sees A retry Fits DEFAULT_ORDER (LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 2000), inside everything above the retrieved context and the tool calls, read from the prompt re-asks the model with the same context and tool history; retrieval and tools are not re-run most chains, and anything with retrieval BEFORE_TOOLS_ORDER (HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 250), between memory and the tool loop the tool calls, recorded during each attempt; not the retrieved context re-runs the tools, so a tool that returned something wrong can return something else tool-heavy chains without retrieval, where a bad tool result is the usual failure

Both positions sit inside chat memory at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 200, so memory records only the answer finally returned.

Session memory

Spring AI 2.1 deprecates MessageChatMemoryAdvisor in favour of the session advisors (SessionAdvisors). Those run in two places: the turn advisor at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 200, and the memory advisor inside the tool loop, at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 1000. Both are outside this advisor's default order. At BEFORE_TOOLS_ORDER, however, the session memory advisor is inside the retry loop, so it sees every attempt and not only the final answer.

At BEFORE_TOOLS_ORDER the attempt's tool traffic never reaches this advisor's prompt, so it is recorded instead: for each attempt, the request's tool callbacks are wrapped, and every call lands in tool_calls with its arguments and result. That position is also outside every advisor at order 0: retrieval re-runs on each attempt, with the judge's feedback in its query, and the judge's user_question does not contain the retrieved context.

Recorded tools

Tools passed as callbacks, through ChatClient.tools(...) or defaultTools(...), are recorded. A tool resolved by name through a ToolCallbackResolver is not. A recorded call that threw is noted as error: <message>, which may differ from the text the model was shown.

docs.title: When a retry asks for a tool
docs.text:
At the default order the advisor is inside the tool loop, and a retry is meant to re-ask the model with the tool results it already has. If the model answers a retry with another tool call, refining stops there and the best answer so far is returned (or DecisionSelfRefineFailedException is thrown, with failOnExhaustedAttempts).

Running that tool would hand the turn back to the tool loop, which re-enters this advisor with no memory of the attempts already made. maxRepeatAttempts could not be kept, and the tools would run again on every round. When a failure is best fixed by calling the tools again, use BEFORE_TOOLS_ORDER, where every retry runs the whole tool loop.

docs.title: Failing hard
docs.text:
By default the advisor returns the best attempt once attempts run out: the one with the most criteria passed net of those failed, the later one on a tie. A later attempt is not necessarily a better one, so the last is not returned just for being last; and an attempt that failFast or an unmet dependency left mostly unjudged passes little, so it does not win by default. Turn that around where shipping a rejected answer is worse than failing:

DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder()
    .judge(judge)
    .maxRepeatAttempts(2)
    .failOnExhaustedAttempts(true)   // throws DecisionSelfRefineFailedException
    .build();

catch (DecisionSelfRefineFailedException ex) {
    log.error("gave up: {}", ex.verdict().summary());
    ex.verdict().failures().forEach(f -> log.error("  {}", f.detail()));
}

docs.title: When judging fails
docs.text:
An outage of the decision model says nothing about the answer. By default the advisor fails open on transient failures: it logs a warning and returns the response it could not judge, rather than failing a chat call whose answer may be fine.

Any other failure, such as a bad API key or an invalid question, is a misconfiguration rather than an outage. It is always rethrown, so it cannot silently turn judging off.

Which failures are transient depends on the provider, and the DecisionModel API has no common exception for it. By default (DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.isTransient) a failure counts when it, or one of its causes, is an IOException, an UncheckedIOException, a TimeoutException or Spring AI's TransientAiException. A provider that reports a rate limit or a server error with an exception of its own is not covered; add its test:

DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder()
    .judge(judge)
    .transientErrorPredicate(((Predicate<Throwable>) DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor::isTransient)
            .or(SystemOneRetryUtils::isTransient))   // System One and Ollama models
    .build();

Where an unjudged answer must never ship, fail closed instead. Every failure of the judging call is then rethrown:

DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder()
    .judge(judge)
    .judgeErrorPolicy(DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.JudgeErrorPolicy.FAIL_CLOSED)
    .build();

The policy applies to whatever judge.judge(...) throws, and that includes the judge's own code checks and appliesWhen predicates, which run inside it. An exception from a check is a bug in the check and is rethrown like any other non-transient failure; but a check that throws something the transient predicate accepts, such as an UncheckedIOException from reading a file, is treated as an outage and the answer is returned unjudged. Keep I/O out of checks.

A criterion the model refuses to answer is not a failure of the call at all: it is an ERROR finding in the verdict, which blocks only when the judge is built with failOnError(true).

docs.title: Ordering with the guardrail advisor
docs.text:
The two compose, and they do different jobs. The recommended setup screens the request before anything else and every reply right next to the model:

.defaultAdvisors(
    DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.input(decisionModel),                   // safety, once per turn
    DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder().judge(judge).build(),        // quality, retries
    DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.output(decisionModel))                  // safety, every attempt

The output guardrail sits inside the self-refine loop, nearer the model. It screens every attempt, so an unsafe draft is replaced by the refusal before it is judged. The input guardrail sits outside it, so it screens what the person wrote rather than a message with the judge's feedback appended. See where the guardrail sits.

Retrying does not help a guardrail: an unsafe answer is not a draft. So a turn the guardrail refuses is final. The refusal is marked in the response context (DecisionGuardrailAdvisor.OUTCOME_CONTEXT_KEY), and the default skipEvaluationPredicate does not judge or retry it.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: adviseStream is unsupported and returns Flux.error(UnsupportedOperationException). A verdict needs the whole answer, so there is nothing useful to emit incrementally.

docs.title: StubDecisionModel
docs.text:
A DecisionModel that answers from a script instead of calling a provider, and records every prompt it was given. It lets you test judges, guardrails and anything else built on the DecisionModel API offline, with no provider and no key.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-decision-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

The artifact also holds PromptField, for assertions on the input a decision model was given, and ScriptedChatModel, a chat model that replies from a script.

docs.title: What to test with it
docs.text:
A real model decides what the answers are. Everything after that is your code: the thresholds, the criteria that depend on each other, the code checks, the hazards' actions. That part is deterministic, and worth testing without a model:

  • that a probability just under a threshold fails a criterion, and just over it passes;
  • that a refused question blocks a guardrail turn rather than passing it;
  • that an advisor retries, and what its retry prompt says;
  • that the right fields reach the model.

What a stub cannot tell you is whether your questions are good. For that, run them against a real model in an integration test, and check their stability with DecisionConsistency.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import static org.springaicommunity.decision.test.StubDecisionModel.score;
import static org.springaicommunity.decision.test.StubDecisionModel.yesNo;

class WeatherJudgeTests {

    private final StubDecisionModel model = new StubDecisionModel();

    @Test
    void failsAnImplausibleAnswerOnPlausibilityAlone() {
        this.model.respondWith(Map.of(
                "helpfulness", score(3.0, 0.9, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0),
                "is_plausible", yesNo(0.03)));

        DecisionVerdict verdict = judge(this.model).judge(
                "What is the weather in Paris?", "It is -255 degrees Celsius in Paris.");

        assertThat(verdict.failures()).extracting(DecisionFinding::name).containsExactly("is_plausible");
        this.model.verify();
    }
}

docs.title: Scripting the answers
docs.text:
A stub answers in one of two ways.

Call by call. respondWith(...) and failWith(...) queue the outcome of one call each, consumed in order. A call with nothing queued fails the test, so an unexpected call cannot pass unnoticed, and verify() fails when a queued outcome was never asked for.

StubDecisionModel model = new StubDecisionModel();
model.respondWith(Map.of("is_plausible", yesNo(0.03)))        // first call
     .respondWith(Map.of("is_plausible", yesNo(0.97)))        // second call
     .failWith(new IllegalStateException("provider down"));   // third call

The same every time. answering(...) gives the same answers to every call, or computes them from the prompt. failing(...) fails every call.

StubDecisionModel steady = StubDecisionModel.answering(Map.of("urgent", yesNo(0.9)));

StubDecisionModel byText = StubDecisionModel.answering(prompt -> {
    Object text = ((FieldsInput) prompt.getInstructions()).getFields().get("text");
    boolean flagged = String.valueOf(text).contains("bomb");
    return Map.of("physical_harm", yesNo(flagged ? 0.95 : 0.01));
});

StubDecisionModel down = StubDecisionModel.failing(new IllegalStateException("provider down"));

Only the questions a prompt asks are answered, so one script can serve prompts that ask for a subset of it. A question the script has no answer for fails the call, as a provider that left a question out would.

docs.title: Building answers
docs.text:
Static factories build each kind of answer:

Factory Builds yesNo(probability) a yes/no answer choice(value, confidence) a choice with a confidence and no probabilities choice(value, confidence, probabilities(...)) a choice with the probability of each option score(value) a score with neither a confidence nor probabilities score(value, confidence, probabilities...) a score with the probability of each level, lowest first refusal(reason) a refusal, for any question 
choice("billing", 0.82, probabilities("billing", 0.9, "technical", 0.1));
score(2.34, 0.51, 0.0, 0.07, 0.52, 0.41);   // a four-level rubric
refusal("policy");

The confidence can be null, which is how to test code against a provider that reports none.

Answers are checked like a provider's

The response is built with the DecisionResponse builder, which rejects a score above its rubric, or probabilities that do not match the number of levels. A scripted answer that could not come from a real model fails the test rather than passing through.

docs.title: Asserting on the prompt
docs.text:
Every prompt is recorded. Read them back with prompts() and lastPrompt():

assertThat(model.prompts()).hasSize(2);
assertThat(model.lastPrompt().getOptions()).isSameAs(options);

To check a prompt at the moment of the call, start the script with expect(). PromptField asserts on one value of the prompt's fields, addressed by a JSON path:

import static org.springaicommunity.decision.test.PromptField.field;

model.expect()
    .andExpect(field("$.assistant_answer").value("It is 15 degrees Celsius in Paris."))
    .andExpect(field("$.tool_calls[0].name").value("weather"))
    .andExpect(field("$.tool_calls.length()").value(1))
    .andExpect(field("$.supporting_context").doesNotExist())
    .respondWith(Map.of("is_plausible", yesNo(0.97)));

value(...) also takes a Hamcrest matcher, such as containsString("Paris"). A broken expectation fails the test with an AssertionError when the call is made.

PromptField reads a fields input, which is what the judge, the guardrail and the chat adapter send. For a text or conversation input, assert on prompt.getInstructions() directly with andExpect(prompt -> ...).

docs.title: ScriptedChatModel
docs.text:
A ChatModel that replies with a scripted sequence of answers and records the prompts it was given. Use it to test an advisor chain end to end:

StubDecisionModel judgeModel = new StubDecisionModel();
judgeModel.respondWith(FAILING).respondWith(PASSING);
ScriptedChatModel chatModel = new ScriptedChatModel(
        "It is -255 degrees Celsius in Paris.", "It is 15 degrees Celsius in Paris.");

String content = ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
    .defaultAdvisors(DecisionSelfRefineAdvisor.builder().judge(judge(judgeModel)).build())
    .build()
    .prompt("What is the weather in Paris?")
    .call()
    .content();

assertThat(content).isEqualTo("It is 15 degrees Celsius in Paris.");
assertThat(chatModel.callCount()).isEqualTo(2);
assertThat(chatModel.userMessageOfCall(1)).contains("Your previous answer was rejected");

Two scripted steps go beyond plain text:

Step The model replies with ScriptedChatModel.toolCall(name, arguments) a tool call, so ChatClient runs its tool loop ScriptedChatModel.afterThinking(thinking, answer) a thinking block as a generation of its own, ahead of the answer

receivedPrompts(), callCount() and userMessageOfCall(index) read back what the model was asked.
